As of 306 AM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: High pressure is currently over Nova Scotia early this 
morning, resulting in broken cloud cover flowing into northern New 
York and Vermont from the west with light and variable winds at the 
surface. Temperatures are expected to continue their gradual fall 
towards the 50s to mid 60s this morning, featuring some isolated 
valley fog. A shortwave trough will reach northern New York from the 
west this afternoon, though the pre-existing drier air mass in place 
and high pressure locked in to our east will keep any resulting 
precipitation limited to a few showers or thunderstorms. As 
temperatures increase into the upper 70s to mid 80s this afternoon, 
models are indicating some modest instability (surface CAPE 500-1000 
J/kg) and precipitable water values approaching 1.25-1.50 inches. 
This could result in a few of the showers or storms offering briefly 
heavy downpours in isolated spots, but we've been dry for days so 
this is not expected to immediately cause issues. Then, another 
mainly dry night tonight with lows in the mid 50s to mid 60s is 
looking likely, a low temperature range that is expected to persist 
each night into the midweek. 

On Monday, the shortwave will shift eastward. Temperatures will be 
able to rise into upper 70s and 80s, increasing surface instability 
(around 1000 J/kg) and producing more widespread showers and 
thunderstorms than Sunday with 50-80% chance of precip in northern 
New York and 5-50% chance of precip across Vermont, highest in the 
afternoon. While we'll lack an upper level feature, precipitable 
water values may approach 1.40-1.60 inches and localized heavier 
downpours could occur. Shower activity should dwindle with sunset, 
though about 20-40% chance of some lingering activity in northern 
New York and southern Vermont. Precipitation amounts are forecast as 
high as 0.25-0.50 inches Monday and Monday night across the 
Adirondacks, likely higher in isolated heavy downpours. Now through 
Monday evening, the probability of reaching a total rainfall of 1 
inch or more is around 25-40% at some of the higher peaks of the 
Adirondacks. We'll want to watch any place that gets consecutive 
days of heavy downpours, particularly across northern New York, but 
the threat is highly conditional. The Weather Prediction Center has 
northern New York outside of the Champlain Valley under Marginal (at 
least 5%, a 1 out of 4 scale) Risk of rainfall exceeding flash flood 
guidance. As of this morning, river forecasts show some slight 
rises, but nothing near bankfull or Action Stage. 

Then on Tuesday, we'll see another trough move through the region, 
though deterministic global models continue to disagree on the 
strength and extent of this feature. The GFS keeps the upper wave 
mostly open, progressive, and aloft, occasionally closing off a 
weaker upper low across southern New York and eventually developing 
a coastal surface low off the mid-Atlantic by late Tuesday night. 
The ICON model is in fair agreement with the GFS. The ECMWF 
continues to push for a strong, closed, vertically stacked low 
pressure system drifting through the Northeast Tuesday and Tuesday 
night. Meanwhile, the Canadian model also favors the GFS's open wave 
on Tuesday, then starts to close and deepen the low pressure like 
the ECMWF does late Tuesday night. Whichever direction we go, 
showers and thunderstorms are looking increasingly likely on Tuesday 
(55-95% chance precip) and Tuesday night (50-80% chance precip). 
Some model solutions are projecting surface CAPE values around 1000-
1500 J/kg. Precipitable water values peak near 1.75 inches on 
Tuesday, so again localized downpours will be possible in surface 
convergence and upper level divergence. If the stronger closed upper 
low solution verifies, we may see more widespread heavy downpours. 
Overall Tuesday-Tuesday night precipitation expectations are 0.25-
1.00" across northern New York (highest amounts in St. Lawrence 
County) and 0.05-0.65" across Vermont (highest amounts in southern 
and south-central Vermont). Any areas that saw heavier downpours on 
Sunday or Monday will need to be watched. By Tuesday, the WPC has 
the Marginal (at least 5%) Risk of excessive rainfall over the 
entire forecast area. Because of all these additional showers, 
thunderstorms, and general moisture/clouds around, highs Tuesday 
will come back down just a couple degrees, in the upper 70s to mid 
80s.

On Wednesday, our main question becomes: how long does the upper 
trough linger across our area? Regardless of the clear model 
differences, most solutions have precipitation lingering through the 
day Wednesday, 55-90% chance of showers and thunderstorms, with 
highest confidence in southern portions of our area, closest to 
forcing. Precipitation likely won't be as convective as previous 
days, though pwats nearing 1.20-1.75 inches are possible. After
